Module 04 › Chapter 4.6 › Overview
Database Replication and Backup Strategies
Ensure high availability, scale reads, and enable safe recovery for MariaDB/MySQL.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

This chapter teaches the mechanics and practical steps: enabling binary logs, creating a replication user, recording the master log position for initial sync, and configuring a slave. You will also learn two backup approaches: logical exports using mysqldump and physical hot backups using mariabackup. Together these tools let you design a recovery plan that balances downtime, storage, and restore speed.

We emphasize production safety: use unique server_id values, restrict replication user access, use --single-transaction for InnoDB when using mysqldump, always run mariabackup's prepare step, and store backups off-site. Practical command examples and a short lab are included so you can reproduce the flow on two VMs.

screens.title: What is Replication and Why Use It?
screens.narratorSegment: Replication is the process of copying data from a primary database server to one or more secondary servers so that multiple copies exist for availability and scale. In MariaDB/MySQL the master writes changes into a binary log and replicas read that log and reapply the changes. This design gives three practical benefits: first, high availability — a slave can be promoted to master to reduce downtime after a failure; second, scalability — read-heavy workloads can use replicas for SELECT queries to offload the primary; third, redundancy — multiple copies reduce risk from a single hardware failure. A concrete example: a web application with 1000 reads per second can keep one master for writes and three read replicas serving application read queries, reducing master load. A common misconception is that replicas are always perfectly in sync; asynchronous replication can lag, so Seconds_Behind_Master may be non-zero during bursts. For critical writes that must be durable across replicas, consider synchronous options or application-level confirmation patterns. Key takeaway: replication helps availability and scale, but you must monitor replication threads and understand eventual consistency. Ask yourself when a small replication lag is acceptable and when your application requires stricter consistency.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.6 › Replication: Definition
Replication — core definition
Replication copies data by reading the master's binary log and applying it on replicas. This creates multiple live copies of the dataset.
High Availability
Promote a replica to master if the primary fails to minimize downtime.
Scalability
Distribute read queries to replicas to reduce master load.
Redundancy
Multiple copies protect against single-server failures.
Key Takeaway

Replication is asynchronous by default; plan for possible lag and monitor Slave_IO and Slave_SQL thread status.

Concrete example
A master receives writes. It appends events to mysql-bin. A replica connects using a replication user and fetches binlog events, applying them so its dataset mirrors the master's changes. After initial sync, the master writes event X, the replica applies X and eventually shows Seconds_Behind_Master returning to zero when caught up.
Common misconception
Replicas are not instant. Asynchronous replication can lag and is not a substitute for tested backups. Relying on replicas as the only data copy risks data loss if the binlog or master state is corrupted.
Check your understanding
  • Why might a read replica report non-zero replication lag during peak traffic?
  • When would you prefer a physical backup over a logical one?

screens.title: Enable Binary Logging and Configure Master
screens.narratorSegment: Preparing a server to act as a master requires a few deliberate configuration steps. First, enable binary logging in /etc/my. cnf under the [mysqld] section by adding log_bin and a unique server_id. The server_id must be a number not used by any other server in the topology. Second, ensure the bind-address allows the slave to connect; in some environments you will use 0.0.0.0 or a specific network interface. After saving my. cnf, restart MariaDB with systemctl restart mariadb to apply changes. Third, create a dedicated replication user that has the REPLICATION SLAVE privilege; grant access only from the known slave IP where possible. Fourth, record the current master status using SHOW MASTER STATUS after obtaining a consistent snapshot — you may lock tables with FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK while you run SHOW MASTER STATUS to ensure a consistent File and Position. Remember to UNLOCK TABLES afterwards. A common error is forgetting to restart the server after editing my. cnf or leaving server_id duplicated across servers. In practice you will perform these steps on the primary and then transfer the data snapshot to the slave. The key safety check is that the master is producing binlog files and your replication user can authenticate remotely.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.6 › Master Configuration
Master: key configuration steps
Follow this step flow to prepare the primary server for replication.
1
Edit /etc/my.cnf: set log_bin = mysql-bin and server_id = 1.
2
Restart MariaDB: sudo systemctl restart mariadb. Verify binlog files exist in the data directory.
3
Create a replication user and grant REPLICATION SLAVE privilege. Restrict host to the slave IP for safety.
4
Lock tables for a consistent snapshot, run SHOW MASTER STATUS, note File and Position, then UNLOCK TABLES.
Safety note

Always use unique server_id values and avoid granting replication to '%' in production. Restrict replication user to specific IPs.

Command examples
# Edit /etc/my.cnf under [mysqld]
log_bin = mysql-bin
server_id = 1

# Restart MariaDB
sudo systemctl restart mariadb

# Create replication user (example)
CREATE USER 'repl_user'@'10.0.0.5' IDENTIFIED BY 'ReplicationP@ssw0rd!';
GRANT REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.* TO 'repl_user'@'10.0.0.5';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

# Capture master position
FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK;
SHOW MASTER STATUS;
UNLOCK TABLES;
Key Takeaway

A correct master config produces binary logs and a reliable File/Position for initializing slaves. Test the replication user can authenticate remotely before configuring the slave.

screens.title: Initialize and Configure the Slave
screens.narratorSegment: Once the master is prepared and you have a consistent snapshot or logical dump, configure the slave to begin replicating. First, set a unique server_id on the slave by editing /etc/my. cnf and restart the service. If you used a mysqldump file, import it to initialize the slave dataset so it matches the master at the recorded File and Position. Next, run the CHANGE MASTER TO command on the slave, specifying MASTER_HOST, MASTER_USER, MASTER_PASSWORD, MASTER_LOG_FILE, and MASTER_LOG_POS using the values you recorded from the master. Start replication with START SLAVE. To verify successful replication, run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G and check that Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are both Yes and monitor Seconds_Behind_Master for lag. A common pitfall is configuring MASTER_LOG_FILE and MASTER_LOG_POS that do not match the dataset state on the slave; this will produce replication errors. Another frequent issue is a network firewall blocking port 3306 between the master and slave. Practically, you will transfer the dump file from master to slave using scp or similar, import it, then run CHANGE MASTER TO with the exact master log coordinates. The final verification is to insert a test row on the master and query the slave to confirm the row appears.

keyIdea.text: Set unique server_id, import initial data snapshot, run CHANGE MASTER TO with master coordinates, START SLAVE, and confirm both replication threads are running.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.6 › Slave Initialization
Slave configuration steps
These steps bring a replica online and connect it to the master binlog stream.
  1. Edit /etc/my.cnf on the slave to set server_id = 2 and restart MariaDB.
  2. Import the initial data snapshot from the master, either via a mysqldump import or a prepared mariabackup copy-back.
  3. Run CHANGE MASTER TO with MASTER_HOST, MASTER_USER, MASTER_PASSWORD, MASTER_LOG_FILE, MASTER_LOG_POS using values from the master snapshot.
  4. Run START SLAVE and then SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G to confirm Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are Yes.
Common mistake

Using incorrect master log coordinates or importing the wrong snapshot state will break replication and require resynchronization.

Example commands
# On slave: set server_id in /etc/my.cnf and restart
sudo systemctl restart mariadb

# Import dump transferred from master
mysql -u root -p test_app_db < /tmp/test_app_db_master_backup.sql

# Configure replication (example)
CHANGE MASTER TO
  MASTER_HOST='192.0.2.10',
  MASTER_USER='repl_user',
  MASTER_PASSWORD='ReplicationP@ssw0rd!',
  MASTER_LOG_FILE='mysql-bin.000001',
  MASTER_LOG_POS=123;

START SLAVE;
SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G
Check

Confirm both Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are Yes and run a test insert on the master to validate replication.

screens.title: Asynchronous Replication & Binlog Types
screens.narratorSegment: MariaDB/MySQL replication is typically asynchronous: the master writes changes to its binary log, and replicas read and apply those changes. The binlog can be recorded in statement-based or row-based formats. Statement-based logging records the S Q L statements that modified data, which is compact but can produce different results if nondeterministic functions are used. Row-based logging records the actual changed rows, ensuring the exact data is replicated but producing larger logs. There is also a mixed mode combining both. Practically, row-based is safer for complex changes and avoids inconsistencies, while statement-based can be smaller for simple, deterministic workloads. Asynchronous replication means there can be a replication lag — replicas may be slightly behind the master. A real example: if a stored procedure uses CURRENT_TIMESTAMP within an UPDATE, statement-based replication may apply a different timestamp on the replica unless deterministic behavior is ensured. A misconception is thinking asynchronous implies unreliable; it is reliable for most systems but requires monitoring and a strategy for critical writes. The takeaway: choose the binlog format based on determinism and size, and monitor Seconds_Behind_Master to make informed decisions about promoting replicas or handling stale reads.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.6 › Binlog Types
Statement-based
Records SQL statements executed on the master.
  • Smaller logs for simple deterministic statements.
  • Can diverge if statements are nondeterministic.
  • Example risk: functions returning different results on replica.
Row-based
Records the actual row changes, ensuring exact data reproduction.
  • Larger logs but more deterministic replication.
  • Preferred for complex updates, stored procedures, and non-deterministic operations.
  • Example: exact changed rows guarantee consistent replica state.
Asynchronous behavior and lag
Replicas may lag; monitor Seconds_Behind_Master. Decide if lag is acceptable for read replicas or if stricter patterns are needed for critical writes.
Key Takeaway

Choose row-based for correctness, statement-based for smaller logs, and monitor lag to understand read consistency boundaries.

screens.title: Create a Replication User & Capture Master Status
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a replication user and capturing the master position are small tasks with big consequences if done incorrectly. The replication user needs the REPLICATION SLAVE privilege so the replica can read the master's binary log. For security, restrict the user to the slave's IP instead of '%' in production. After creating the user and flushing privileges, you must capture the master's current binary log file and position. For a consistent snapshot, run FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK to stop writes briefly, then SHOW MASTER STATUS to read File and Position. Note those exact values for the slave configuration, then UNLOCK TABLES so writes resume. A common misconception is that SHOW MASTER STATUS without a locked snapshot is sufficient; for transactional consistency, lock or use consistent dumping methods. Here is an example sequence you will run: create the user, flush privileges, lock tables, show master status, and unlock. When you speak these steps, think of the master as producing a stream of events — the File and Position mark the point where the replica must begin applying events to match the master's state. Always verify the replication user can connect from the slave using simple mysql client authentication before starting slave threads.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.6 › Replication User & Status
Create replication user
Grant minimum privileges and restrict by host.
CREATE USER 'repl_user'@'10.0.0.5' IDENTIFIED BY 'ReplicationP@ssw0rd!';
GRANT REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.* TO 'repl_user'@'10.0.0.5';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;
Security tip

Avoid granting replication access from all hosts; use a CIDR or fixed IP for the slave to reduce exposure.

Capture master coordinates
Lock tables, show status, and release locks.
FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK;
SHOW MASTER STATUS;
-- Note the File and Position values
UNLOCK TABLES;
Key Takeaway

Record the exact File and Position under a consistent snapshot. These coordinates seed the slave to the correct point in the master's binlog stream.

screens.title: Logical Backups with mysqldump
screens.narratorSegment: mysqldump is a logical backup tool that exports databases as S Q L statements you can later run to recreate the schema and rows. It is ideal for small to medium datasets, cross-version portability, and quick schema exports. The typical pattern is sudo mysqldump -u root -p myapp_db > backup. sql. For consistent snapshots on InnoDB tables use --single-transaction so the dump runs inside a transaction and avoids table locks. For all-database exports use --all-databases, and for restores you run mysql -u root -p myapp_db < backup. sql. Be aware that mysqldump may be slow and resource-intensive for very large databases and can cause downtime if not used with appropriate options. A concrete example from the chapter: perform a single-transaction dump of test_app_db before initializing a slave. A common misconception is that logical dumps are always safe for large production systems; in reality, they are often impractical for terabyte-sized datasets. When using mysqldump for replication initialization, transfer the dump file securely to the slave via scp then import it before running CHANGE MASTER TO. The takeaway: mysqldump is simple and portable, but match the tool to database size and recovery time objectives.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.6 › mysqldump
Logical backup: mysqldump
Export database objects and data as SQL statements for flexible restoration.
# Backup a single database with consistent snapshot for InnoDB
sudo mysqldump -u root -p --single-transaction myapp_db > /tmp/myapp_db_backup_2023-10-27.sql

# Restore
sudo mysql -u root -p myapp_db < /tmp/myapp_db_backup_2023-10-27.sql
Practical note

For busy InnoDB systems, always prefer --single-transaction to avoid locking. For very large datasets prefer physical backups.

When to use mysqldump
  • Small to medium databases where portability matters.
  • Schema-only exports or migrations between versions.
  • Initializing a replica when dataset size is manageable.
Key Takeaway

mysqldump is easy and portable but can be slow and resource heavy for large production datasets. Use it with --single-transaction for consistent InnoDB dumps.

screens.title: Physical Backups with mariabackup
screens.narratorSegment: mariabackup performs hot physical backups by copying InnoDB data files while the server is running. This is the recommended approach for large and busy production databases because it avoids long locks and produces faster restores. The workflow is three steps: perform a backup with mariabackup --backup --target-dir=..., prepare the backup with mariabackup --prepare to make the copied files consistent, and restore by stopping MariaDB, cleaning the data directory, running mariabackup --copy-back, and fixing file ownership with chown -R mysql:mysql. The prepare step is essential; skipping it will result in inconsistent data on restore. Physical backups are dependent on the exact MariaDB version and architecture, so you should not assume compatibility across major versions. A concrete example: run sudo mariabackup --backup --target-dir=/var/backups/mariadb/full_2023-10-27 --user=root --password='rootpass', then prepare the backup and test a restore on a staging server. A common mistake is storing backups only on the database host, which makes them vulnerable to the same failure. Always copy backups off-site and test restores regularly. The key insight is that physical backups enable fast recovery for large datasets but require careful preparation and testing.

keyIdea.text: Run mariabackup --backup, then --prepare, then --copy-back with correct permissions; always test restores and store backups off-site.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.6 › Physical Backups
mariabackup workflow
Hot backup, prepare, and restore steps for InnoDB data files.
# Full backup
sudo mariabackup --backup --target-dir=/var/backups/mariadb/full_2023-10-27 --user=root --password=''

# Prepare backup
sudo mariabackup --prepare --target-dir=/var/backups/mariadb/full_2023-10-27

# Restore (dangerous: stops server and removes data dir)
sudo systemctl stop mariadb
sudo rm -rf /var/lib/mysql/*
sudo mariabackup --copy-back --target-dir=/var/backups/mariadb/full_2023-10-27
sudo chown -R mysql:mysql /var/lib/mysql
sudo systemctl start mariadb
Warning

Restoring with copy-back deletes the data directory. Only restore on a prepared target and ensure you have off-site copies.

When to use mariabackup
  • Very large databases where mysqldump is impractical.
  • Busy systems requiring minimal locking and faster restores.
  • Environments where physical file-level restores are acceptable.
Key Takeaway

Physical backups are fastest for restores at scale but require careful prepare and version compatibility checks. Always test restores on a staging host.

screens.title: Designing a Comprehensive Backup Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A backup tool alone is not a strategy. Design a policy with frequency, retention, off-site storage, monitoring, and regular restore tests. Frequency balances recovery point objective and storage: daily full backups are common, with hourly incrementals if you need tighter recovery points. Retention defines how long you keep backups: examples include 7 daily, 4 weekly, and 12 monthly backups to cover operational and compliance needs. Store copies off-site to protect against local disasters; off-site can be object storage or separate data centers. Monitor backup job success, disk utilization, and alert on failures. And crucially, test restores on a staging server: a backup that was never restored may be corrupt. The chapter suggests monitoring and testing as the most overlooked step. A concrete example policy: daily full mariabackup with weekly snapshot replication to off-site storage, with automated alerts for failures and monthly restore drills. A common misconception is that having replicas negates the need for backups—replicas do not substitute for tested backups because they can replicate logical mistakes or corruptions. The outcome you should aim for is a documented plan that is automated, monitored, and exercised by restores.

Backup policy components
Define the who, what, where, when, and how of your backups.
Frequency
Daily fulls; hourly incrementals if needed.
Retention
7 daily, 4 weekly, 12 monthly as an example plan.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Setup Replication and Run mysqldump
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough mirrors the lab activity. Begin by provisioning two VMs that can reach each other on port 3306. On both VMs install MariaDB and complete mysql_secure_installation. On the master: edit /etc/my. cnf to enable log_bin and server_id=1, restart MariaDB, create a test database and a users table, insert sample rows, create the replication user restricted to the slave IP, and capture master status under a read lock. Export the test database using mysqldump with --single-transaction to /tmp and then transfer it to the slave via scp. On the slave: set server_id=2 in my. cnf, restart MariaDB, import the dump to initialize the dataset, then run CHANGE MASTER TO using the master's IP and recorded File and Position, and START SLAVE. Verify that SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G reports Slave_IO_Running: Yes and Slave_SQL_Running: Yes and that a test insert on the master appears on the slave. A common problem is importing the dump after configuring the master coordinates; import first, then point the slave at the correct coordinates. After you validate replication, practice a mysqldump restore to verify recovery procedures. This sequence teaches the full lifecycle from configuration to verification.

keyIdea.text: Follow the lab steps to provision two VMs, configure master and slave, initialize the slave with a mysqldump, and verify replication by inserting test data.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.6 › Lab Walkthrough
Master steps (summary)
  1. Install MariaDB and run mysql_secure_installation.
  2. Edit my.cnf: log_bin=mysql-bin, server_id=1. Restart service.
  3. Create database test_app_db and table users; insert sample rows.
  4. Create repl_user@'slave_ip' with REPLICATION SLAVE and FLUSH PRIVILEGES.
  5. FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK; SHOW MASTER STATUS; UNLOCK TABLES.
  6. mysqldump --single-transaction test_app_db > /tmp/test_app_db_master_backup.sql and scp to slave.
Slave steps (summary)
  1. Edit my.cnf: server_id=2. Restart MariaDB.
  2. Import the dump: mysql -u root -p test_app_db < /tmp/test_app_db_master_backup.sql.
  3. Run CHANGE MASTER TO with recorded MASTER_LOG_FILE and MASTER_LOG_POS.
  4. START SLAVE; SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G and confirm both threads are Yes.
  5. Test: insert a row on master and verify it appears on the slave.
Lab tip

Transfer the dump file with scp and verify file integrity before importing. Import first, then point the slave at the recorded master coordinates.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Replication and Backup Problems
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding frequent problems helps you recover faster. One common replication failure is missing REPLICATION SLAVE privilege for the replication user; the slave cannot authenticate and the input and output thread will remain stopped. Another frequent cause is firewall rules blocking port 3306 between master and slave, so always verify network connectivity. Duplicated server_id values across servers will break replication because each server must be uniquely identified. For mysqldump users, forgetting --single-transaction can lead to table locks during long dumps and application downtime. For mariabackup, skipping the --prepare step yields inconsistent files on restore. Another risk is storing backups on the same host as the database—if the server dies you lose both data and backups. Finally, untested backups are a false sense of security: a backup is only valid if you can restore it. A practical troubleshooting flow: check systemd logs, confirm binlog files exist, test replication user authentication locally and remotely, run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G for replication errors, check firewall rules, and verify disk space. The closing question to ask: when you encounter replication stopped, what exact error does SHOW SLAVE STATUS reveal and what next corrective action will you perform?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.6 › Troubleshooting
Common problems and checks
Use this checklist to triage replication and backup issues.
Privileges
Ensure replication user has REPLICATION SLAVE and run FLUSH PRIVILEGES if needed.
server_id
Confirm unique server_id values across all servers in topology.
Network
Verify port 3306 is open and reachable between master and slave.
Binlog presence
Confirm master is producing mysql-bin files and SHOW MASTER STATUS returns data.
Slave status
Use SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G to inspect Slave_IO_Running, Slave_SQL_Running, and Last_Error.
Backups
Always test restores; don’t keep backups only on the database host.
Scenario question

If SHOW SLAVE STATUS shows Slave_IO_Running: No, check replication user auth and network connectivity before any further reconfiguration.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Replication & Backups (1)
screens.narratorSegment: These core concepts will help you remember the essentials. Replication is copying changes from a primary to secondary servers for availability and scale. Master-slave replication places writes on the master and applies changes on slaves. The Binary Log is the master's record of data-modifying events that replicas read to keep in sync. The server_id is a unique identifier every server needs in a replication topology. CHANGE MASTER TO is the S Q L command the slave uses to configure the master's address and starting binlog coordinates. SHOW SLAVE STATUS lets you inspect replication health, showing whether input and output and S Q L threads are running and the current lag. Hold these definitions in mind as you configure systems: understanding the role of the binlog and how the slave consumes it is the basis for correct replication. Finally, remember to restrict the replication user and test replication after setup.

fullNarratorScript:
In production systems, data integrity and quick recovery are non-negotiable. This lesson focuses on practical replication and backup techniques for MariaDB and MySQL that keep services available, enable scalable reads, and preserve data against failures. You will learn why replication provides redundancy and read scalability, how binlogs drive asynchronous replication, and which backup tools to use depending on database size and uptime needs. We’ll show concrete commands to enable binary logging, create a replication user, record the master log position, configure a slave, and verify replication health. Then we’ll contrast logical backups made by mysqldump with physical, file-level backups made by mariabackup, and explain the crucial prepare and restore steps. Finally, we’ll outline a production-ready backup policy: frequency, retention, off-site storage, monitoring, and the single most important habit—regular restore testing. By the end you’ll understand not only how to perform these tasks, but when each technique is appropriate and what common mistakes to avoid. Think about a recent outage you’ve seen: could a tested backup and a promoted replica have shortened that downtime?

These objectives map to practical LFCE skills you will demonstrate. First, you will explain why replication improves availability, supports read scaling, and provides data redundancy. You should be able to give a concrete example of promoting a slave after a master failure. Second, you will configure a MariaDB/MySQL server to act as a master: enable binary logging, set a unique server_id, restart the service, and create a replication user with appropriate privileges. Third, you will capture a consistent master snapshot and note the binary log file and position as the starting point for a slave. Finally, you will configure a slave: set server_id, apply the change master command, start replication threads, and verify that both input and output and S Q L threads are running. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the steps. These are hands-on outcomes: you will type commands, inspect status output, and resolve common permission or network issues. The final verification is that the slave shows replication running and stays within expected lag while you insert test data on the master.

This second objectives panel focuses on backups and a recoverable policy. First, you will run consistent logical backups using mysqldump and understand when to use the --single-transaction flag to avoid table locks on InnoDB. You will practice restoring a dump into an existing database and understand options that drop and recreate databases during restore. Second, you will perform a physical hot backup using mariabackup: run the backup, run the prepare step to make files consistent, and practice a safe restore including stopping the server and restoring file permissions. Third, you will design a backup cadence: daily fulls, periodic incrementals, defined retention windows, and off-site copies. Fourth, you will implement monitoring and regular restore tests. The milestone is practical: perform a full backup and a restore to a fresh instance and report that data integrity is preserved. These are the operations that reduce recovery time objective and prove your backups work.

Replication is the process of copying data from a primary database server to one or more secondary servers so that multiple copies exist for availability and scale. In MariaDB/MySQL the master writes changes into a binary log and replicas read that log and reapply the changes. This design gives three practical benefits: first, high availability — a slave can be promoted to master to reduce downtime after a failure; second, scalability — read-heavy workloads can use replicas for SELECT queries to offload the primary; third, redundancy — multiple copies reduce risk from a single hardware failure. A concrete example: a web application with 1000 reads per second can keep one master for writes and three read replicas serving application read queries, reducing master load. A common misconception is that replicas are always perfectly in sync; asynchronous replication can lag, so Seconds_Behind_Master may be non-zero during bursts. For critical writes that must be durable across replicas, consider synchronous options or application-level confirmation patterns. Key takeaway: replication helps availability and scale, but you must monitor replication threads and understand eventual consistency. Ask yourself when a small replication lag is acceptable and when your application requires stricter consistency.

Preparing a server to act as a master requires a few deliberate configuration steps. First, enable binary logging in /etc/my. cnf under the [mysqld] section by adding log_bin and a unique server_id. The server_id must be a number not used by any other server in the topology. Second, ensure the bind-address allows the slave to connect; in some environments you will use 0.0.0.0 or a specific network interface. After saving my. cnf, restart MariaDB with systemctl restart mariadb to apply changes. Third, create a dedicated replication user that has the REPLICATION SLAVE privilege; grant access only from the known slave IP where possible. Fourth, record the current master status using SHOW MASTER STATUS after obtaining a consistent snapshot — you may lock tables with FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK while you run SHOW MASTER STATUS to ensure a consistent File and Position. Remember to UNLOCK TABLES afterwards. A common error is forgetting to restart the server after editing my. cnf or leaving server_id duplicated across servers. In practice you will perform these steps on the primary and then transfer the data snapshot to the slave. The key safety check is that the master is producing binlog files and your replication user can authenticate remotely.

Once the master is prepared and you have a consistent snapshot or logical dump, configure the slave to begin replicating. First, set a unique server_id on the slave by editing /etc/my. cnf and restart the service. If you used a mysqldump file, import it to initialize the slave dataset so it matches the master at the recorded File and Position. Next, run the CHANGE MASTER TO command on the slave, specifying MASTER_HOST, MASTER_USER, MASTER_PASSWORD, MASTER_LOG_FILE, and MASTER_LOG_POS using the values you recorded from the master. Start replication with START SLAVE. To verify successful replication, run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G and check that Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are both Yes and monitor Seconds_Behind_Master for lag. A common pitfall is configuring MASTER_LOG_FILE and MASTER_LOG_POS that do not match the dataset state on the slave; this will produce replication errors. Another frequent issue is a network firewall blocking port 3306 between the master and slave. Practically, you will transfer the dump file from master to slave using scp or similar, import it, then run CHANGE MASTER TO with the exact master log coordinates. The final verification is to insert a test row on the master and query the slave to confirm the row appears.

MariaDB/MySQL replication is typically asynchronous: the master writes changes to its binary log, and replicas read and apply those changes. The binlog can be recorded in statement-based or row-based formats. Statement-based logging records the S Q L statements that modified data, which is compact but can produce different results if nondeterministic functions are used. Row-based logging records the actual changed rows, ensuring the exact data is replicated but producing larger logs. There is also a mixed mode combining both. Practically, row-based is safer for complex changes and avoids inconsistencies, while statement-based can be smaller for simple, deterministic workloads. Asynchronous replication means there can be a replication lag — replicas may be slightly behind the master. A real example: if a stored procedure uses CURRENT_TIMESTAMP within an UPDATE, statement-based replication may apply a different timestamp on the replica unless deterministic behavior is ensured. A misconception is thinking asynchronous implies unreliable; it is reliable for most systems but requires monitoring and a strategy for critical writes. The takeaway: choose the binlog format based on determinism and size, and monitor Seconds_Behind_Master to make informed decisions about promoting replicas or handling stale reads.

Creating a replication user and capturing the master position are small tasks with big consequences if done incorrectly. The replication user needs the REPLICATION SLAVE privilege so the replica can read the master's binary log. For security, restrict the user to the slave's IP instead of '%' in production. After creating the user and flushing privileges, you must capture the master's current binary log file and position. For a consistent snapshot, run FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK to stop writes briefly, then SHOW MASTER STATUS to read File and Position. Note those exact values for the slave configuration, then UNLOCK TABLES so writes resume. A common misconception is that SHOW MASTER STATUS without a locked snapshot is sufficient; for transactional consistency, lock or use consistent dumping methods. Here is an example sequence you will run: create the user, flush privileges, lock tables, show master status, and unlock. When you speak these steps, think of the master as producing a stream of events — the File and Position mark the point where the replica must begin applying events to match the master's state. Always verify the replication user can connect from the slave using simple mysql client authentication before starting slave threads.

mysqldump is a logical backup tool that exports databases as S Q L statements you can later run to recreate the schema and rows. It is ideal for small to medium datasets, cross-version portability, and quick schema exports. The typical pattern is sudo mysqldump -u root -p myapp_db > backup. sql. For consistent snapshots on InnoDB tables use --single-transaction so the dump runs inside a transaction and avoids table locks. For all-database exports use --all-databases, and for restores you run mysql -u root -p myapp_db < backup. sql. Be aware that mysqldump may be slow and resource-intensive for very large databases and can cause downtime if not used with appropriate options. A concrete example from the chapter: perform a single-transaction dump of test_app_db before initializing a slave. A common misconception is that logical dumps are always safe for large production systems; in reality, they are often impractical for terabyte-sized datasets. When using mysqldump for replication initialization, transfer the dump file securely to the slave via scp then import it before running CHANGE MASTER TO. The takeaway: mysqldump is simple and portable, but match the tool to database size and recovery time objectives.

mariabackup performs hot physical backups by copying InnoDB data files while the server is running. This is the recommended approach for large and busy production databases because it avoids long locks and produces faster restores. The workflow is three steps: perform a backup with mariabackup --backup --target-dir=..., prepare the backup with mariabackup --prepare to make the copied files consistent, and restore by stopping MariaDB, cleaning the data directory, running mariabackup --copy-back, and fixing file ownership with chown -R mysql:mysql. The prepare step is essential; skipping it will result in inconsistent data on restore. Physical backups are dependent on the exact MariaDB version and architecture, so you should not assume compatibility across major versions. A concrete example: run sudo mariabackup --backup --target-dir=/var/backups/mariadb/full_2023-10-27 --user=root --password='rootpass', then prepare the backup and test a restore on a staging server. A common mistake is storing backups only on the database host, which makes them vulnerable to the same failure. Always copy backups off-site and test restores regularly. The key insight is that physical backups enable fast recovery for large datasets but require careful preparation and testing.

A backup tool alone is not a strategy. Design a policy with frequency, retention, off-site storage, monitoring, and regular restore tests. Frequency balances recovery point objective and storage: daily full backups are common, with hourly incrementals if you need tighter recovery points. Retention defines how long you keep backups: examples include 7 daily, 4 weekly, and 12 monthly backups to cover operational and compliance needs. Store copies off-site to protect against local disasters; off-site can be object storage or separate data centers. Monitor backup job success, disk utilization, and alert on failures. And crucially, test restores on a staging server: a backup that was never restored may be corrupt. The chapter suggests monitoring and testing as the most overlooked step. A concrete example policy: daily full mariabackup with weekly snapshot replication to off-site storage, with automated alerts for failures and monthly restore drills. A common misconception is that having replicas negates the need for backups—replicas do not substitute for tested backups because they can replicate logical mistakes or corruptions. The outcome you should aim for is a documented plan that is automated, monitored, and exercised by restores.

This hands-on walkthrough mirrors the lab activity. Begin by provisioning two VMs that can reach each other on port 3306. On both VMs install MariaDB and complete mysql_secure_installation. On the master: edit /etc/my. cnf to enable log_bin and server_id=1, restart MariaDB, create a test database and a users table, insert sample rows, create the replication user restricted to the slave IP, and capture master status under a read lock. Export the test database using mysqldump with --single-transaction to /tmp and then transfer it to the slave via scp. On the slave: set server_id=2 in my. cnf, restart MariaDB, import the dump to initialize the dataset, then run CHANGE MASTER TO using the master's IP and recorded File and Position, and START SLAVE. Verify that SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G reports Slave_IO_Running: Yes and Slave_SQL_Running: Yes and that a test insert on the master appears on the slave. A common problem is importing the dump after configuring the master coordinates; import first, then point the slave at the correct coordinates. After you validate replication, practice a mysqldump restore to verify recovery procedures. This sequence teaches the full lifecycle from configuration to verification.

Understanding frequent problems helps you recover faster. One common replication failure is missing REPLICATION SLAVE privilege for the replication user; the slave cannot authenticate and the input and output thread will remain stopped. Another frequent cause is firewall rules blocking port 3306 between master and slave, so always verify network connectivity. Duplicated server_id values across servers will break replication because each server must be uniquely identified. For mysqldump users, forgetting --single-transaction can lead to table locks during long dumps and application downtime. For mariabackup, skipping the --prepare step yields inconsistent files on restore. Another risk is storing backups on the same host as the database—if the server dies you lose both data and backups. Finally, untested backups are a false sense of security: a backup is only valid if you can restore it. A practical troubleshooting flow: check systemd logs, confirm binlog files exist, test replication user authentication locally and remotely, run SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G for replication errors, check firewall rules, and verify disk space. The closing question to ask: when you encounter replication stopped, what exact error does SHOW SLAVE STATUS reveal and what next corrective action will you perform?

These core concepts will help you remember the essentials. Replication is copying changes from a primary to secondary servers for availability and scale. Master-slave replication places writes on the master and applies changes on slaves. The Binary Log is the master's record of data-modifying events that replicas read to keep in sync. The server_id is a unique identifier every server needs in a replication topology. CHANGE MASTER TO is the S Q L command the slave uses to configure the master's address and starting binlog coordinates. SHOW SLAVE STATUS lets you inspect replication health, showing whether input and output and S Q L threads are running and the current lag. Hold these definitions in mind as you configure systems: understanding the role of the binlog and how the slave consumes it is the basis for correct replication. Finally, remember to restrict the replication user and test replication after setup.

This final set of concepts captures backup mechanics and safety practices. mysqldump creates logical backups as S Q L statements and is suitable for portability and smaller datasets; use the --single-transaction option for InnoDB to avoid long locks during dumps. mariabackup performs physical hot backups of InnoDB data files and requires a prepare step to make the copied files consistent before restore. The --prepare step is non-optional: skipping it yields inconsistent restores. Off-site storage and retention windows protect against local disasters, and monitoring plus scheduled restore tests validate your backups. Remember common safety checks: run FLUSH PRIVILEGES after creating users, ensure unique server_id values, open port 3306 between master and slave, and never store the only backup on the same server as the data. These practices reduce the chance of prolonged outages and ensure recoverability when incidents occur.
